items.title: Scholars still can’t define religion. Here’s why
items.summary: Scholars of religion still can’t agree on what religion is, and Andrew Henry, creator of Religion for Breakfast, thinks that tells us something. In this conversation with Jonny Thomson, he explains why he looks at what religious practices do rather than what they claim, why a stadium chant and a church creed may be closer than they seem, and why “true Christianity” is harder to pin down than its defenders suggest. They also take on common debate points, from the historical Jesus to Tom Holland’s claim that Western values are Christian at heart. This video Scholars still can’t define religion. Here’s why is featured on Big Think .

items.title: AI Is Destroying the Trust Between Writers and Readers
items.summary: One evening last fall, a middle-aged couple, heads bent in conversation, approached the table where I sat signing books. “Go ahead,” the woman urged. Speaking softly, her husband explained that he had Parkinson’s disease. Although he hadn’t read my novel The Weight of Ink , it was his understanding that it featured a character with Parkinson’s who chose to die by assisted suicide rather than endure her decline. He had some objections. I was horrified—not because I’d written something that offended him, but because I hadn’t. Helen Watt, the character with Parkinson’s in The Weight of Ink , does not, in fact, end her own life. I didn’t know for certain where his misunderstanding had originated, but I had a guess. Just a few weeks earlier, I’d asked ChatGPT a few questions about my novel; it responded to certain queries with this false rendition of Helen’s plotline. Ever since, I’d worried that the misrepresentation might somehow have a real-life impact. Now, it seemed, it had. Any working writer can expect to be called out for their choices; critique is part of the terrain. As a novelist, I’ve been chided for details including a character’s self-defeating relationship decisions and an incorrect date for a 17th-century full moon. But that evening in late 2025 was the first time I’d been called to account for something I hadn’t actually written. And even as I explained to the couple before me that what they’d seen online was incorrect, I wondered: How many other people had been similarly misled? The proliferation of artificial intelligence has raised new fears about the long-term viability of writers’ already tenuous profession, as the technology infiltrates prize-winning writing, scrapes books for learning material, and perhaps erodes readers’ attention spans. But alongside that upheaval, another subtler sort of destruction is under way. AI-enabled meddling is turning the reader-writer connection into a hall of fun-house mirrors, and threatening to break the trust that is essential to that bond. In the Monty Python sketch “ Bookshop ,” a customer requests a progressively more absurd list of copycat Charles Dickens works. Does the shop have a copy of Knickerless Knickleby ? Or perhaps titles by one Charles Dikkens (“that’s Dikkens with two K ’s”)? The customer’s insistence on the legitimacy of these books gradually drives John Cleese’s bookshop-clerk character into a frenzy. What was delightfully preposterous decades ago is now uncomfortably familiar. With a blizzard of literary fakery overtaking the world of books, discerning what’s real requires vigilance on the part of readers. [ Read: The worst thing about AI writing ] In 2017, when I published The Weight of Ink , there was no other book by that title in the English language. This remained the case until the fall of 2025. Since then, at least five other novels with titles identical to mine have become available on Amazon, three of them published in the space of three weeks. Several other books with nearly identical titles also are listed for sale. I don’t know whether, or to what extent, AI was used in creating these books whose content otherwise seems to bear little or no resemblance to my novel; I found only one that contains an up-front disclaimer acknowledging AI authorship. But as Will Oremus noted in a recent Atlantic article , new-book releases on Amazon skyrocketed after 2022, around the time that AI models became widely accessible to the public. “That’s probably not because humans suddenly dedicated themselves en masse to the written word,” Oremus wrote. Similarly, it’s hard to believe that this profusion of Weight of Ink s is the result of an abrupt, hyperspecific surge of entirely human creativity. In some ways, I felt lucky to have just my title copied; in late 2024, my friend the novelist Daphne Kalotay discovered that her author page on Amazon featured a brand-new novel that she hadn’t written. This book, which Kalotay described as “an AI hallucination based on descriptions of Russian Winter ,” her 2010 novel, had been paired with a title and cover from a completely unrelated book from decades earlier and was being sold under her name. “What was most unsettling,” Kalotay told me, “was how difficult it was to prove it was garbage.” In the end, the Authors Guild, an advocacy organization of which Kalotay is a member—and which has launched a certification program designed to distinguish human-authored books from those generated by AI—succeeded in getting Amazon to delete the book from her author page. This sort of scam is now everywhere in publishing. Generating book-length texts using AI costs almost nothing, and Amazon lets individuals upload a maximum of six books a week, allowing for endless churn. Anyone selling AI-generated texts need only mislead a few customers per book—whether by using an existing work’s title or an author’s name—in order to turn a profit . “Amazon spends a lot of time and effort trying to prevent these books from getting posted,” Mary Rasenberger, the CEO of the Authors Guild, told me, “but it’s always a game of catch-up.” The fakery cuts both ways: Writers are also being bombarded by AI-generated phishing attempts in the guise of emails from appreciative readers. Such emails are so pervasive that, like many of my peers, I now sometimes hesitate to even open my reader mail. Each of these notes begins personally, only to morph into an offer of paid marketing services. A recent example begins: “Dear Rachel, This feels scary to send, but I’m trusting my heart today.” The subsequent description of my work’s ostensible impact (“Your words found me at a time when I was quietly falling apart”) is followed by a pitch for a marketing plan to promote my novella, I Was Here . These promotion schemes are, of course, more fakery; the Authors Guild maintains a running list of such scams, in which writers who sign up see their money vanish . [ Read: Deepfakes are coming for your bank account ] Although fraudulent emails in writers’ inboxes usually purport to be from readers, some are sent under the names of published writers. (Some are also brazenly posthumous; a friend of mine received compliments on her memoir from “Charlotte Bronte.”) Earlier this month, a writer I don’t know forwarded me an email he’d received from someone claiming to be me. In that email, “Rachel Kadish” reached out to him “author to author” to express interest in his work. Below my alleged signature on the email were links to my actual website, as well as to my Amazon and Goodreads pages. I reached out to “Rachel Kadish” to ask them to explain their purpose in using my identity. The reply I received—an ingratiating and incoherent piece of clearly AI-generated text—acknowledged the impersonation before going on to explain that the ruse had all been for my benefit. (“My intention was to connect with fellow authors and introduce them to your work, as I believe authors discovering and supporting one another can be valuable.”) The best part was the sign-off: “Going forward, I will communicate under my own name and will not use your identity to contact other authors. Sincerely, Rachel.” This is a new, bleak kind of fraud, different from the literary deception of earlier eras, in which scandals at least had something to teach us. Consider The Education of Little Tree : Published in 1976 as the true autobiographical story of a Cherokee boy, the book was revealed in 1991 to be the work of a former member of the KKK. Or Binjamin Wilkomirski’s Fragments : Memories of a Wartime Childhood , whose exposure as a fake gave rise to the term Wilkomirski syndrome for the phenomenon of non-Jews posing as Holocaust survivors. These scandals revealed not only the writers’ lies but also the degree to which readers’ desire for certain stories can blind us. There was human folly and frailty to learn from. A few recent scandals, involving prize-winning writing that was suspected of being AI-generated, likewise force us to stare

items.title: Exclusive Double Cover Reveal of Two Forthcoming Forrest Gander Titles
items.summary: Electric Literature is pleased to reveal the covers of The Weight of a Frozen Moment and Dune Lines: New and Selected Poems by Forrest Gander, which will be published respectively on April 6, 2027 by Milkweed and April 27, 2027 by New Directions. You can pre-order your copies here and here . The Weight of a Frozen Moment From Pulitzer Prize-winning author Forrest Gander comes a poignant exploration of intimate human and ecological bonds. In a small intentional community in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains, two sisters—Maya and Mira—grow up sharing explorations, secrets, and the sense that their lives are unfolding in parallel. But as adolescence pulls Mira away, first subtly and then irrevocably, Maya must remake herself alone: through grief and family tragedy, through a journey to Karnataka to honor the anniversary of their father’s death, and through an ever-deepening bond with the place that helped shape her. Strikingly lyrical and quietly devastating, Forrest Gander’s poetic restraint and his detailed attention to the natural world imbues the landscape with a gravitational pull on the narrative. The Sierra Nevada is witness, anchor, and the ground on which the sisters find their way back to each other and to an even more expansive sense of belonging. A meditation on place, identity, and the strength of the ties that endure, The Weight of a Frozen Moment offers unexpected grace in demonstrating what it means to be separate and inseparable. Here is the cover, designed by Mary Austin Speaker: Forrest Gander: Mary Austin Speaker, who designed the cover for The Weight of a Frozen Moment , values vintage artwork precisely because it comes from an era before AI—out of respect for those artists who painstakingly made art by hand. This cover image, which might have started as a black and white photograph, isn’t generically pretty. In fact, it’s hard to tell whether we’re looking at a painting, drawing, lithograph, or photograph. It has the dreamy in-betweenness of a metaphor, partly real, partly imagined. And then there’s something about the way the heavy, fissured rock cushions the sheerness of the waterfall, the way the forest’s darkness seems more preparatory than foreboding that suggests the quality of memory and of the signal events that orient Maya, the main character in the novel. As her sister drifts into adulthood and her father falls ill, she has to reckon with a self she can’t fully enter. Then again, although it doesn’t gesture toward the transnational dimension of the book, the particular landscape in which the characters live—the Sierra Nevada foothills overlooking the Yuba River Canyon and Tahoe National Forest—may itself be the main character, and the cover captures that just as well. Mary Austin Speaker: For the cover of Forrest Gander’s exquisitely rendered novel, I wanted to evoke the feeling of finding a private place in the woods, like the sisters at the center of the story do, and thought a waterfall would be a great way to symbolize that feeling of discovery, awe, and the rushing-and-stillness of time (and the gravity of memory) that Gander articulates so beautifully across the span of the book. Because images of waterfalls can tend toward the cliché (and this is particularly true of photographs), I looked for something extra-saturated with something painterly about it. I ultimately settled on a lithograph of Latourelle Falls printed by the Wesley Andrews company in 1935 for its slightly askew colors, and for how the forest hugs the edges of the image. I have collected lithographic postcards for years precisely because of their in-betweenness. They were printed in an era before color photography and hand-painted, so they become a pastiche of the real and the imagined, which lends them an eerie power. It must have something to do with the nature of memory and how it becomes part of who we are, in all its embellishments, as the characters in the book discover, and how certain scenes from our life persist vividly while everything around them darkens. Dune Lines: New and Selected Poems What is an ethical life? An erotic life? A life underpinned by awe? By grief? What is it to recognize oneself as comprised of others, human and not? What hasn’t this poet lavished his “gorgeous attention” on? Gathered from 40 years of published books, the Pulitzer-Prize winning poet Forrest Gander’s Dune Lines offers such poignance: of tenderness, tragedy, phenomenological inquiry, and the almost sustaining particularities of love. His poems are worldly in scale, but intimate in scope, fusing geological and human time. Dune Lines contains a wide-ranging selection of many of Gander’s best-loved poems, revealing how he has charted his utterly distinctive course in contemporary poetry. Here is the cover, designed by Rodrigo Corral and Giacomo Girardi: Forrest Gander: Dune Lines , my third consecutive book with a cover designed by Rodrigo Corral Studios—this time, a collaboration between Corral and Giacomo Girardi—is gorgeously minimal but suggestive. A single repeated vertical gesture, calling to mind cymatics or oscilloscope traces, swells, and narrows until the eye starts to hear rhythm. When I first saw it I thought of Bridget Riley’s early black-and-white Op Art meeting the sensual, formal strictures of Ellsworth Kelly’s drawings. The shapes could be reeds or ribs or a seismograph recording. Or, of course, dune lines reassembled bolt upright. That would be especially appropriate for sections included from the book Mojave Ghost , which records a hike along the San Andreas fault into the Mojave Desert, where I was born. It’s all suggestiveness, and that’s exactly what a book of selected and new poems, gathered from 40 years, would want as its face. The cover also might be taken to enact the throb and ebb, the rising and falling music of the many poetic sequences included in the book. Shifting takes on a theme, on an event, a query proposed from several perspectives. Even a visual representation of the act of breathing—which is an integral element of my poetic process. Rodrigo Corral : The cover for Dune Lines is an undulating rhythm of movement and stillness. The shifting line weights, representative of the dunes, meet in the middle to become a skull, encapsulating the cyclical nature of life, grief, memory, and what it means to be human in relation to nature and its geological timeline. The post Exclusive Double Cover Reveal of Two Forthcoming Forrest Gander Titles appeared first on Electric Literature .

items.title: A “theory” has a special meaning in science
items.summary: Whenever someone tells you that they “have a theory,” you’re probably a mix of curious and skeptical, and with good reason. Most often, you’re going to hear a wild tale that’s a mix of true and dubious facts, possible but suspicious links between them, guesses that range from informed hypotheses to extravagant speculations, and a story about how they’ve introduced one (or more) modifications to the standard story of how things are known work. This is almost always followed with an important caveat at the end: that they have no proof of this, as it’s “only a theory.” In common, informal use, the word theory is tossed around as casually as words like: hypothesis, guess, hunch, idea, or gut feeling, among others. In other words, when someone shares their pet theory with you in this regard, you might humor them by considering it, but you’d be well within the bounds of reasons to dismiss their “theory” without putting too much weight behind it. But some people take this informal definition of theory — as a mere hypothesis, guess, or idea — and apply it to our most vaunted of scientific theories as well. They’ll argue that Darwinian evolution, the Big Bang, gravitation, and quantum mechanics are just “theories” as well, and therefore shouldn’t be taken to be facts. They’ll argue that theories were overturned in the past, and so they’re justified in not believing today’s theories that are well-accepted as part of the scientific consensus. Some will even point to now-discredited scientific ideas, like the theory of phlogiston, Jungian psychology, or the Lamarckian theory of evolution, or to speculative ideas that have “theory” in the title, like Grand Unified Theory or string theory, to argue that many of our best, currently-accepted theories will eventually turn out to be wrong. But this is a fundamentally dishonest argument, as any scientist will be quick to realize. Here’s what everyone should know about what the word “theory” truly means: in everyday conversation, in scientific circles, in mathematics, and beyond. This animation shows the breakup of supercontinent Gondwanaland, which itself was a large subsection of Pangaea at one point, into the smaller continents of South America, Antarctica, Africa, Australia, as well as components of other continents that are recognizable, such as Arabia and India. The theory of plate tectonics and continental drift is so successful because of the evidence that supports it. Credit : B. Goldberg/Quora, modified by E. Siegel The colloquial use of “theory” is just an “idea” In our everyday life, the word “theory” that we hear bandied about is simply the same as the word “idea.” We make no distinction between whether that idea is: a good one that has merit or a bad one that is contradicted by reality, an old one that was long ago formulated by someone else or a novel one, a valid one that has successful explanatory power or an invalid one that makes incorrect predictions, or a scientific one that can be tested and either verified and validated or contradicted and ruled out, or a non-scientific, unfalsifiable one. In our everyday life, we all have that friend, neighbor, or relative who has rather kooky ideas — something akin to “the Moon is a hologram” or “a secret race of lizard people is controlling the Earth” — and likely refers to their idea as a theory, just as surely as scientists refer to Einstein’s relativity as a theory. The much-ballyhooed idea of panpsychism , although often called a theory, falls into this category of an untestable notion with no evidence behind it. In all of these cases, we’re only talking about an idea: the initial germ of a hypothesis. Hypotheses may yet grow into fully-fledged scientific theories, and indeed what eventually become scientific theories typically start off as mere hypotheses or ideas, but simply having an idea doesn’t mean you have a good idea, a valid idea, or even a scientific idea, much less a scientific theory. In order to go from an idea to a scientific theory, there are multiple ways the idea in question must be scrutinized. Touted as UFO lights, this 2011 photograph over Liverpool does, in fact, document a series of lights in an oddly unnatural-appearing configuration, but this is by no means compelling evidence for aliens. In fact, it’s simply an image looking up at the lights of Radio City Tower under dark, foggy conditions, which does not constitute scientific evidence for either UFOs or aliens. Credit : dreese/Wikimedia Commons Is the idea plausible? Based on what we already know, if this idea turned out to be correct, would it undermine or conflict with observations, measurement, and data that we already possess? If so, then the idea — at least, the idea as it currently stands — is not plausible, and that’s a non-started for it becoming a scientific theory. Does the idea have explanatory power? Based on the idea you’re considering, are there phenomena, measurements, or observations that are presently not explained by what we know, that could be explained by this new idea? If not, then this idea has no hope of becoming a scientific theory, as “predictive power” is the key reason and motivation for the formulation of scientific theories in the first place. Is the idea testable? This is, in many regards, the biggest one: is there some definitive test that can be performed to test this new idea? Is there some way we can compare this idea to the currently favored, prevailing scientific theory it’s seeking to supplant or replace, where we can put these predictions side-by-side, where they’ll differ from one another, and where nature itself will be the arbiter? If not — if this idea is not scientifically testable — then there never was any scientific merit to it at all. (It doesn’t have to be a “practical with current technology” test, but it does have to be a “possible given the constraints and physical limitations of our Universe” test.) There are other facets to this idea that might appear nice on the surface — whether the idea is elegant, natural, simple , etc. — but it’s really only these three points of plausibility, explanatory power, and testability that make an idea scientific or not. Unless you can test and evaluate this idea based on the evidence you can gather, the measurements you can make, the experiments you can perform and the observations you can undertake, it is not a scientific idea. This four-panel animation shows the individual galaxies present within Abell 2744, Pandora’s Cluster, alongside the X-ray data from Chandra (red) and the lensing map constructed from gravitational lensing data (blue). The mismatch between the X-rays and the lensing map, as shown across a wide variety of X-ray emitting galaxy clusters, is one of the strongest indicators favoring the presence of dark matter. The Bullet Cluster, as well as other galaxy clusters, exhibit similar features. Credit : X-ray: NASA/CXC/ITA/INAF/J.Merten et al, Lensing: NASA/STScI; NAOJ/Subaru; ESO/VLT, Optical: NASA/STScI/R.Dupke; Animation by E. Siegel All scientific theories exist within a “framework” for exploration There are a great many ideas that never make it to the “accepted, valid scientific theory” state, but that nevertheless wind up with the word “theory” attached to them. That’s because, well before something is sufficiently tested to know whether it’s valid or invalid, we have to tease out its consequences so that we know what to look for in terms of evaluating it. items.title: How to find your way through 2,600 years of philosophy
items.summary: One of the biggest problems any new learner faces is that overwhelming feeling of standing on the shoreline looking out to sea. You want to learn astrophysics, zoology, or economics — where do you start? What ideas come first? Which thinkers are core and which are super niche? Philosophy is no different. If anything, it’s worse. Because a lot of people know a few philosophers or have read a few books and quotes. Millions have watched the first season of True Detective . But when faced with the vastness of “Philosophy,” it’s like standing on a tiny sloop in the Pacific Ocean, being told to swim. Sure, you can take a course. There are hundreds of great intro books out there. My entire professional raison d’être is to fix this problem. But now we’ve got another way. Big Think has decided to create “The Chart of Western Philosophy.” It lays out some 2,600 years of Western thought on a single timeline, from Thales to Žižek, so you can see at a glance where everyone sits and how they connect. Here you will find the schools and movements that shaped philosophy, from the Milesians and the Stoics to the Existentialists and the Post-Structuralists, each tagged to show which branches of philosophy it cares about most, and the lines of teacher, student, and influence that tie them all together. Around the edges are short guides to the major schools and the texts worth reading. The Chart of Western Philosophy To celebrate the poster’s release and to find out more about it, I spoke with Big Think’s resident artist and poster-maker extraordinaire , Ben Gibson, who is also cofounder of the infographic poster company Pop Chart. What factors did you consider in whom to include and whom not to? Pop Chart has always been really interested in trying to portray the scope of big ideas through detailed infographics of subject matters like science, literature, and culture. But when we’re in the research phase of projects, the net will often scoop up interesting things we later realize don’t quite fit the core idea. An example of this popping up during the development of the Chart of Western Philosophy was the Sophists of ancient Greece. Nowadays, “sophist” is a derogatory term for someone who uses clever deceptions or logical fallacies to manipulate others. But in Greece in the fifth and fourth centuries BC, Sophists were a sort of tutor who specialized in rhetoric, public speaking, and arete (virtue or excellence). They were philosophy-adjacent, but really more like classical life coaches, who charged a fee for their services. Plato, in his dialogues, calls Sophists these teachers of deception. This sort of criticism from Plato and other influential figures led to the way the term is used today. What other options did you consider in making this, and why select this one? A big issue was the organizing principle of the content and layout. We strongly considered organizing the content around the main branches of philosophy: metaphysics, epistemology, logic, ethics, aesthetics, and political philosophy. This makes a lot of sense conceptually, except that it runs into a big logistical problem of categorization: most, if not all, philosophy movements are not just about one branch of philosophy, but multiple, in different ratios. This led us to organize the content in a timeline format, and also to devise a system of symbols for the branches, placed next to each movement, indicating which branch of philosophy is its primary concern, its secondary concern, and so on. What problems did you have with this? The scope of it was a figuratively and literally big problem, as it usually is when trying to get across a big, sweeping idea in one infographic design. For some influential movements, there are seemingly limitless offshoots. For Platonism alone: Early Platonism/Plato’s Academy, Academic Skepticism, Middle Platonism, Neoplatonism, Carolingian Platonism, Realist Platonism, and many, many more. This sort of thing is an editorial issue as well as a practical one. Editorial, because which philosophy movements are most important, and which are more tertiary? Practical, because how many philosophy movements can we possibly fit on one printed piece of paper? What is the most interesting or surprising thing you learned about philosophy from making it? The cattiness of philosophers! From classical philosophy on through to the modern era, philosophers are regularly dropping sick burns on one another — either philosophical burns, or really just personal attacks. Some examples: Schopenhauer vs. Hegel Schopenhauer called Hegel a “flat-headed, insipid, nauseating, illiterate charlatan” who produced “a monument to German stupidity.” Voltaire vs. Rousseau On receiving Rousseau’s essay arguing that society corrupts people, Voltaire wrote: “I have received, Sir, your new book against the human race… Never has so much wit been employed to make us stupid; reading your work makes one want to walk on all fours.” Nietzsche vs. everyone Nietzsche referred to Kant as “the most deformed concept-cripple of all time,” and said Socrates belonged “by origin to the lowest folk” — maybe an insult related to Socrates being a street orator. You can find “The Chart of Western Philosophy” in Big Think’s online store . This article How to find your way through 2,600 years of philosophy is featured on Big Think .

items.title: You’re allowed to be happy. In fact, you have a duty to be.
items.summary: Albert Camus and Simone de Beauvoir were having a drink when de Beauvoir asked how anybody can be happy in a world so full of misery. How can they laugh and drink and dance when millions of people are being murdered and abused? It’s a good question, and one I’m sure many of us have asked at one time or another. Unless you’ve made a deliberate effort to avoid even a glimpse of the news, you know that the world contains vast and intense suffering: wars, murders, and abuse, of course, but also sickness, famine, and natural disaster. How is it ever okay to clink glasses of champagne while children are dying? How can we so easily sleep at night knowing that someone, somewhere, is being tortured? And then Camus gave his answer: “Happiness exists, and it’s important; why refuse it?” Camus argued that refusing joy does nothing to cure the misery in the world. It merely adds your misery to the total sum. It makes us less capable of defeating it. A Brief for the Defense In 2005, the poet Jack Gilbert published a poem called “A Brief for the Defense,” where he imagined a defendant accused of having joy. The world contains famine and torture and children dying in places you will never see. And so how can you dare to laugh? How can you be happy while others are suffering? Gilbert’s answer, like Camus’s, is to say that if suffering exists and you respond by extinguishing your own joy, then suffering has produced two losses rather than one. First, there is the pain itself: the bullet, the scream, the anguish. And then, there is the echo — the suffering that comes from focusing too long on the suffering. We shouldn’t allow misery to win twice. In fact, he even goes further than this, further than most people are comfortable with. Gilbert says delight isn’t only permitted, but that you have a duty to feel delight. To deny yourself joy when the world contains so much horror would allow horror to set the terms. When so much of the world is dark, we are responsible all the more for bringing in some light. Gilbert and Camus were not saying that we should ignore suffering, or that we shouldn’t try to help. Rather, they were saying that our pain doesn’t relieve the world’s pain. In fact, Camus argued the opposite: Accepting happiness makes us better equipped to fight for it. For our tomorrow In 1946, among the ruins of Nazi Germany, the philosopher Karl Jaspers described something similar to de Beauvoir’s unease but on a grander scale: what he called “metaphysical guilt.” This is not the guilt of anything you did, but it’s the guilt of simply surviving when others have not. It’s that unbearable guilt of being here when others could not be. It’s the happiness you enjoy that others cannot. Jaspers argued we cannot will this feeling away, but we can learn from it. We can learn that we are bound to all humans who have ever existed and will ever exist. When we adopt this metaphysical view, we see ourselves in solidarity with the species. History is a network, and our lives are webbed together. In my living, I represent life. I am writing this article in November, when many countries around the world mark a remembrance for those who died in conflict. And, in the UK at least, there’s a line that’s used a lot. It’s from the war memorial at Kohima: “For your tomorrow, we gave our today.” So, use it. Use the today that we have been gifted. Find all the joy that those who gave their lives could not. Camus, Gilbert, and Jaspers are getting at a similar thing. Pausing to appreciate the sacrifices of the past and present is important and respectful. Working as much as is reasonable to alleviate suffering is moral. But living as fully and happily as we can is a kind of duty. We should laugh loudly for those who cannot. We should enjoy the world’s wonders because so many are deprived of access to them. We should squeeze as much goodness from life as possible because that isn’t possible for millions. As the activist Dan Savage put it, “During the darkest days of the AIDS crisis, we buried our friends in the morning, we protested in the afternoon, and we danced all night. The dance kept us in the fight because it was the dance we were fighting for.” This article You’re allowed to be happy. In fact, you have a duty to be. is featured on Big Think .
